questions: Do you have numbness or tingling in either hand or arm?
Do you have weakness in either hand or arm?
Are your symptoms worse on one side than the other?
Do you have neck pain that radiates into an arm?
Have you noticed difficulty with balance or walking?
Have you had any recent injury to your neck, shoulder, arm, or hand?
Do you have diabetes?
Have you ever been diagnosed with multiple sclerosis or another neurological condition?
Do you have an involuntary tremor or shaking in either hand?
Do you have involuntary jerking or twitching of either arm or hand?
Do you have pain in either hand, wrist, elbow, or shoulder?
Do you have difficulty with fine hand movements, such as buttoning clothes or using utensils?
Do your hand movements become abnormal or worsen when you are asked to perform a task?
Do the abnormal movements improve when you are distracted?
Did the tremor begin suddenly, over days or weeks, rather than gradually over months or years?
Is the tremor present when the affected hand is completely at rest?
Is the tremor mainly present when holding the hand out or using it?
Does the tremor lessen after drinking alcohol?
Does anyone in your family have a similar tremor?
Do you have stiffness or slowness of movement?
Do you have changes in handwriting, such as progressively smaller writing?
Do you have reduced sense of smell or loss of smell?
Do you have episodes in which the affected hand seems to move or act without your control?
orders: Perform a focused movement-disorders neurological examination, documenting whether the tremor is present at rest, with posture, or during action; assessing finger tapping and hand opening/closing for bradykinesia, passive-wrist rigidity, and gait with arm swing.
Review the medication and substance history, specifically looking for dopamine-blocking drugs, stimulants, excessive caffeine, valproate, lithium, and β-agonists.
MRI brain with and without contrast, including diffusion-weighted imaging, susceptibility-weighted imaging, and thin-slice sequences through the corpus callosum and medial frontal/parietal regions.

Formal neurological examination for cortical signs, including apraxia, cortical sensory loss, neglect, intermanual conflict, grasp reflex, and assessment for asymmetric rigidity, dystonia, and bradykinesia.
EEG to assess for focal seizures presenting as involuntary unilateral hand activity.

Amyloid-β and phosphorylated-tau biomarkers, preferably via cerebrospinal-fluid analysis (Aβ42/40 ratio, total tau, and p-tau), to determine whether the corticobasal syndrome is due to Alzheimer disease pathology.
FDG-PET brain imaging to characterize the asymmetric frontoparietal hypometabolism and assess for an alternative neurodegenerative pattern.
served: finger tapping for bradykinesia and decrement
gait observation including turning and doorways
medication review (neuroleptics, antiemetics, valproate, calcium-channel blockers, lithium)
reflexes, plantar responses and frontal release signs
dystonic posturing of the hand or foot
alien limb / limb levitation with the eyes closed
lumbar puncture / CSF (cells, protein, Abeta42/40, total tau, p-tau)
